overview: Majapahit, founded in eastern Java in 1293, was the last great Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of the archipelago. Under Hayam Wuruk and his minister Gajah Mada it claimed overlordship from Sumatra to the Moluccas and set the pattern that Indonesia's founders looked back to.

items.text: The Nagarakretagama, a poem by Mpu Prapanca finished in 1365, describes the court, the royal progress and the lands that sent tribute.
Red brick temples and gateways at Trowulan, and terracotta figures and piggy banks from the capital.
Wayang shadow plays and gamelan are named in Majapahit texts and carved on its reliefs.
Javanese rice bought the cloves, nutmeg and mace of the Moluccas, which Majapahit ships carried west.
Chinese cash coins were the currency; missions went to the Ming court, and Chinese and Muslim traders lived in the ports.
Shiva and the Buddha were worshipped together; the court poem Sutasoma's line Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, unity in diversity, is Indonesia's motto.
The realm was a mandala of vassals around a divine king, held by ritual and tribute more than by garrisons.
Indonesia's founders invoked Majapahit's reach when they drew the nation's borders.
Its Hindu-Javanese culture lives on in Bali, where nobles and priests moved as Islam spread in Java.

fall.text: The kingdom shrank after Hayam Wuruk's death in 1389 and a civil war; the Muslim sultanate of Demak took the last Majapahit capital around 1527.
